places.name: Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium
places.foundedNote: Oppidum Ubiorum after Agrippa resettled the Ubii (c. 38 or 19 BC); colonia AD 50

status.t: Ara Ubiorum, altar of Rome and Augustus
colonia named after Agrippina the Younger

places.summary: Ubian town raised to a colony at the request of Agrippina, who was born there. Capital of Lower Germany and of Postumus's Gallic empire; Constantine bridged the Rhine to the fort of Divitia (Deutz) c. 310. The Dionysus mosaic and the Praetorium foundations survive.

places.name: Bonna
places.foundedNote: Drusus's Rhine fleet base; fortress from c. AD 35
places.summary: Legionary fortress of 25 ha on the Rhine, held by I Germanica and then for two centuries by I Minervia. Drusus is said to have bridged the Rhine here (Florus 2.30).

places.name: Novaesium
places.summary: Site of a dozen successive camps since Drusus. The Koenen camp, excavated 1887-1900, became the textbook plan of a stone legionary fortress (VI Victrix, c. 70-104).

places.name: Vetera
places.foundedNote: Augustan base for Drusus's campaigns c. 13-12 BC

status.t: Vetera I destroyed; Vetera II built nearby

places.summary: Double fortress opposite the Lippe mouth, launching point for Drusus and Germanicus into Germany. Vetera I was besieged and destroyed in the Batavian revolt (69-70); Vetera II, now under the Rhine's changed bed, held XXX Ulpia Victrix.

places.name: Colonia Ulpia Traiana
places.summary: Trajanic colony of 73 ha beside Vetera II, the only colony in Lower Germany besides Cologne; abandoned after Frankish attacks c. 275 for a fortified core. Now an archaeological park.

places.name: Noviomagus Batavorum
places.foundedNote: Augustan base on the Hunerberg c. 19 BC; Batavian Oppidum Batavorum
places.summary: Oppidum Batavorum, burned by the Batavians in 70; the legionary fortress of X Gemina (71-104) and then a Trajanic municipium. Tile stamps of IX Hispana from here feed the debate on that legion's fate.

places.name: Mogontiacum
places.foundedNote: double fortress founded by Drusus c. 13 BC
places.summary: Fortress at the Main confluence, headquarters of the Upper German army. The Drususstein cenotaph honours Drusus, who died in 9 BC. Saturninus's revolt broke out here in 89; Severus Alexander was murdered nearby at Vicus Britannicus in 235.

places.name: Argentoratum
places.foundedNote: Drusan fort; legionary fortress from c. 17
places.summary: Fortress of VIII Augusta for three centuries. Julian's 13,000 men defeated perhaps 35,000 Alamanni under Chnodomarius outside it in August 357, capturing the king (Amm. 16.12).

places.name: Vindonissa

status.t: fortress of XIII Gemina, then XXI Rapax and XI Claudia

places.summary: The only legionary fortress in Switzerland. Its rubbish dump (Schutthügel) preserved wooden writing tablets, leather and textiles in waterlogged layers.

places.name: Augusta Vindelicum
places.foundedNote: Augustan base after the Alpine war of 15 BC
places.summary: Capital of Raetia on the Via Claudia Augusta. An altar of 260 found in 1992 records a victory over the Iuthungi and names Postumus as emperor, revealing Raetia's adhesion to the Gallic empire.

places.name: Castra Regina
places.foundedNote: fortress dated by the gate inscription of 179
places.summary: Fortress of III Italica on the Danube's northernmost bend, completed in 179; parts of the Porta Praetoria stand in the city. The Bavarian dukes later made it their capital.

places.name: Lauriacum
places.summary: Fortress of II Italica and late bishopric of Noricum Ripense. Its town law fragment (lex Lauriacensis) survives; Severinus withdrew the Danube Romans here in the 470s-480s (Eugippius).

places.name: Iuvavum
places.summary: Claudian municipium of Noricum on the Salzach. The Vita Severini records its sack by the Heruli in the 470s.

places.name: Virunum
places.summary: Claudian capital of Noricum on the Zollfeld, with a large amphitheatre found in 1998. It replaced the hilltop emporium of the Magdalensberg.

places.name: Magdalensberg
places.foundedNote: Noric hill settlement and Roman trading post
places.summary: Hilltop seat of the Noric kingdom, possibly Noreia, where Italian merchants from Aquileia traded Noric iron from c. 100 BC; inscribed walls record orders for iron rings and anvils. Abandoned when Claudius founded Virunum.

places.name: Ovilava
places.summary: Town that became a colony under Caracalla and the capital of Noricum Ripense after Diocletian.

places.name: Batavis
places.summary: Fort at the confluence of the Inn and Danube named after its Batavian garrison. Eugippius tells how its last soldiers sent to Italy for their pay and were found dead in the river.

places.name: Arae Flaviae
places.foundedNote: founded c. 73 during the annexation of the Agri Decumates
places.summary: Flavian foundation on the upper Neckar after Cn. Pinarius Cornelius Clemens's campaign (73-74), giving the name of the Flavian altars to the new Agri Decumates.

places.name: Saalburg
places.summary: Auxiliary fort on the Upper German limes, rebuilt in full in 1897-1907 at Kaiser Wilhelm II's expense as a showpiece of Roman frontier archaeology.

places.name: Kalkriese
places.summary: Pass between the Kalkrieser Berg and the Great Moor where coin finds (none later than AD 9) and a Germanic turf wall point to the destruction of Varus's three legions in September AD 9.

places.name: Londinium
places.foundedNote: founded c. 47-50 at the Thames bridge
places.summary: Bridge town founded after the conquest, burned by Boudica in 60/61, then capital of Britain with a basilica of 2 ha and a fort at Cripplegate. The Bloomberg tablets include the earliest dated document from Britain (8 January 57).

places.name: Camulodunum
places.foundedNote: fortress of XX 43-49; Colonia Claudia Victricensis 49
places.summary: Capital of Cunobelinus, taken by Claudius in person with elephants in 43. The colony's temple of Claudius was the last stand of the veterans against Boudica (Tac. Ann. 14.31-32).

places.name: Verulamium
places.summary: Catuvellaunian centre that Tacitus calls a municipium when Boudica sacked it. Alban, Britain's first martyr, died here in the 3rd or early 4th century; Germanus of Auxerre visited his shrine in 429.

places.name: Eboracum

status.t: fortress of IX Hispana, then VI Victrix

places.summary: Fortress of IX and VI Victrix and capital of northern Britain. Septimius Severus died here on 4 February 211; Constantius I died here on 25 July 306 and his troops acclaimed Constantine.

places.name: Deva

status.t: fortress of II Adiutrix, then XX Valeria Victrix

places.summary: Fortress on the Dee, 20% larger than other British fortresses, perhaps intended as a base for the conquest of Ireland. Its elliptical building is unique.

places.name: Isca Silurum
places.summary: Fortress of II Augusta in Silurian territory, with the most complete visible amphitheatre, barracks and baths in Britain; Arthurian legend later attached itself to it via Geoffrey of Monmouth.

places.name: Glevum
places.foundedNote: fortress at Kingsholm c. 49; colonia c. 97
places.summary: Fortress against the Silures, then one of four British coloniae, founded under Nerva for veterans.

places.name: Lindum

status.t: fortress of IX, then II Adiutrix

places.summary: Fortress on the Fosse Way-Ermine Street junction, converted into a colony in the 90s. Its Newport Arch is the only Roman gate in Britain still used by traffic.

places.name: Viroconium Cornoviorum
places.summary: Fortress for the Welsh campaigns, then the fourth largest town in Britain. Timber halls built over the baths basilica show occupation into the 6th century.

places.name: Calleva Atrebatum

status.t: capital of the client king Togidubnus?

places.summary: Atrebatic town with complete walls that was abandoned rather than built over, giving a full town plan; its small 4th-century building may be a church.

places.name: Aquae Sulis
places.summary: Hot-spring sanctuary of Sulis Minerva. The sacred spring yielded 130 lead curse tablets asking the goddess to punish thieves of cloaks and coins.

places.name: Isca Dumnoniorum
places.summary: Fortress of II Augusta c. 55-75, its bath-house found under the cathedral close; then capital of the Dumnonii.

places.name: Corinium Dobunnorum
places.summary: Second largest town of Roman Britain and probably the capital of Britannia Prima; a column dedicated by the governor L. Septimius was found there.

places.name: Rutupiae
places.summary: Landing place of the Claudian invasion, monumentalised by a four-way marble arch c. 85 as the gateway to Britain. Later a Saxon Shore fort, held by II Augusta according to the Notitia.

places.name: Dubris
places.foundedNote: fort of the Classis Britannica c. 130
places.summary: Fleet base of the Classis Britannica with a surviving lighthouse (pharos) on the cliffs and the 'Painted House' of c. 200.

places.name: Inchtuthil
places.modern: Inchtuthil, Perth and Kinross, United Kingdom
places.summary: Agricolan fortress on the Tay, abandoned unfinished c. 86/87 when II Adiutrix was withdrawn. The garrison buried about 875,000 iron nails rather than leave them.

places.name: Vindolanda
places.summary: Stanegate fort whose waterlogged deposits have yielded over 1,700 ink writing tablets (c. 90-120): a birthday invitation from Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, strength reports, and the soldiers' word for the Britons, 'Brittunculi'.

places.name: Segedunum
places.foundedNote: fort at the eastern end of Hadrian's Wall
places.summary: Fort at the eastern terminal of Hadrian's Wall, fully excavated and displayed.

places.name: Luguvalium
places.summary: Fort on the Eden founded by Cerialis in 72/73 and anchor of the Stanegate; later the civitas capital of the Carvetii.

places.name: Coria
places.summary: Fort and supply town where Dere Street crossed the Tyne. The Corbridge Lion and a hoard of lorica segmentata plates came from here.

places.name: Trimontium
places.summary: Fort below the three Eildon Hills on Dere Street whose pits yielded cavalry parade helmets and a mass of military equipment (Curle 1911).

places.name: Maiden Castle
places.foundedNote: Iron Age hillfort of the Durotriges
places.summary: The largest Iron Age hillfort in Britain. Wheeler's 'war cemetery' (1936), including a skeleton with a ballista bolt in the spine, is linked to Vespasian's campaign, though the dramatic massacre narrative is now doubted.

places.name: Branodunum
places.foundedNote: Saxon Shore fort, mostly of c. 270-290
places.summary: Fort of the Saxon Shore under the comes litoris Saxonici; fort of the Dalmatian cavalry (Equites Dalmatae) in the Notitia.

places.name: Gariannonum
places.foundedNote: Saxon Shore fort, mostly of c. 270-290
places.summary: Fort of the Saxon Shore under the comes litoris Saxonici; walls stand to 4.5 m; Notitia's equites Stablesiani.

places.name: Othona
places.foundedNote: Saxon Shore fort, mostly of c. 270-290
places.summary: Fort of the Saxon Shore under the comes litoris Saxonici; site of Cedd's chapel (c. 654) built from its stones.

places.name: Regulbium
places.foundedNote: Saxon Shore fort, mostly of c. 270-290
places.summary: Fort of the Saxon Shore under the comes litoris Saxonici; early 3rd-century fort of cohors I Baetasiorum.

places.name: Portus Lemanis
places.foundedNote: Saxon Shore fort, mostly of c. 270-290
places.summary: Fort of the Saxon Shore under the comes litoris Saxonici; fort slumped downhill by landslips.

places.name: Anderitum
places.foundedNote: Saxon Shore fort, mostly of c. 270-290
places.summary: Fort of the Saxon Shore under the comes litoris Saxonici; oval fort; Saxons massacred its Britons in 491 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle).

places.name: Portus Adurni
places.foundedNote: Saxon Shore fort, mostly of c. 270-290
places.summary: Fort of the Saxon Shore under the comes litoris Saxonici; walls almost complete, with a Norman keep in a corner.

places.name: Carnuntum
places.summary: Fortress and capital of Upper Pannonia on the Amber Road crossing of the Danube. Marcus Aurelius wrote part of his Meditations here; Septimius Severus was proclaimed emperor here on 9 April 193; the Tetrarchic conference of 308 met here.

places.name: Vindobona
places.summary: Fortress of X Gemina under the Innere Stadt of Vienna. Aurelius Victor says Marcus Aurelius died here in March 180 (others say Sirmium).

places.name: Brigetio
places.summary: Fortress of I Adiutrix. Valentinian I died here on 17 November 375 of a stroke while shouting at Quadic envoys (Amm. 30.6).

places.name: Aquincum
places.summary: Fortress of II Adiutrix and capital of Lower Pannonia, where Hadrian served as governor (107). A water organ (hydraulis) of 228 was found in the fire brigade's hall of the civil town.

places.name: Savaria
places.summary: Claudian colony on the Amber Road and birthplace of Martin of Tours (316).

places.name: Scarbantia
places.summary: Flavian municipium on the Amber Road from Aquileia to Carnuntum.

places.name: Poetovio
places.foundedNote: fortress of VIII Augusta from c. 15
places.summary: Fortress on the Drava where the Danubian legions declared for Vespasian in 69 (Tac. Hist. 3.1); later a Trajanic colony with several Mithraea. Constantius Gallus was arrested here in 354.

places.name: Emona
places.summary: Augustan-Tiberian colony on the route from Aquileia to the Danube, with a precisely gridded plan. Theodosius was welcomed here in 388 after defeating Maximus.

places.name: Siscia
places.summary: Pannonian Segestica, captured by Octavian in 35 BC as the base of his Illyrian war. It had an imperial mint from Gallienus and was the capital of Pannonia Savia.

places.name: Sirmium
places.summary: Danubian residence of Galerius and Licinius and capital of Illyricum, called 'mother of cities' by Ammianus. Birthplace of Probus, Decius and others; four church councils met here (351-358). Its surrender to the Avars in 582 after a two-year siege opened the Balkans.

places.name: Mursa
places.summary: Hadrianic colony on the Drava. The battle of Mursa (28 September 351), where Constantius II defeated Magnentius, was one of the bloodiest of the century (Zonaras: 54,000 dead).

places.name: Cibalae
places.summary: Pannonian town where Constantine defeated Licinius in October 316. Birthplace of Valentinian I and Valens.

places.name: Singidunum
places.foundedNote: Celtic Scordiscan oppidum; legionary fortress from c. 86
places.summary: Scordiscan oppidum on the Danube-Sava confluence and fortress of IV Flavia Felix (Kalemegdan). Start of the Via Militaris to Constantinople. Jovian was born here.

places.name: Viminacium
places.foundedNote: fortress of VII Claudia from c. 57
places.summary: Capital of Moesia Superior and fortress of VII Claudia, with its own provincial coinage dated by a local era from 239. Destroyed by Attila in 441 and refounded by Justinian.

places.name: Naissus
places.summary: Junction town on the Via Militaris. Claudius II crushed a huge Gothic host near it in 268/269. Birthplace of Constantine (c. 272), whose villa at Mediana lies outside it; Priscus saw its ruins full of bones in 448.

places.name: Serdica
places.summary: Thracian city refounded by Trajan as Ulpia Serdica, capital of Aurelian's inner Dacia. Constantine reportedly said 'Serdica is my Rome'; Galerius issued his edict of toleration here in April 311.

places.name: Ratiaria

status.t: capital of Dacia Ripensis, fortress of XIII Gemina

places.summary: Trajanic colony on the Danube that became the capital of Dacia Ripensis and base of XIII Gemina after Aurelian abandoned Dacia. Its arms factory (fabrica) and bishop Palladius (an Arian condemned at Aquileia in 381) are known.

places.name: Oescus
places.summary: Fortress of V Macedonica and Trajanic colony. Constantine built a 2.4 km bridge across the Danube from here to Sucidava in 328.

places.name: Novae
places.foundedNote: fortress of VIII Augusta c. 45, then I Italica
places.summary: Fortress of I Italica for four centuries, excavated by Polish and Bulgarian teams. Theodoric the Amal made it his residence before leaving for Italy in 488.

places.name: Nicopolis ad Istrum
places.foundedNote: founded by Trajan after the first Dacian war
places.summary: Trajan's 'victory city', organised as a Greek polis though on the Latin side of the language line. Ulfilas and his Gothic Christians settled near it in 348.

places.name: Durostorum
places.foundedNote: fortress of XI Claudia from c. 106
places.summary: Fortress of XI Claudia on the Lower Danube. Birthplace of Aetius (c. 391); the soldier Dasius was martyred here c. 303 for refusing to play the Saturnalia king.

places.name: Troesmis
places.summary: Fortress of V Macedonica until 167, then a municipium whose charter bronzes surfaced on the antiquities market in 2008. Later the base of II Herculia.

places.name: Noviodunum
places.summary: Fleet base near the Danube delta where Valens crossed on a pontoon bridge in 369 and met Athanaric in midstream to make peace (Amm. 27.5).

places.name: Tomis
places.summary: Greek port where Ovid spent his exile from AD 8 until his death c. 17, writing the Tristia and Epistulae ex Ponto. Later capital of Scythia Minor; a huge mosaic floor of a warehouse survives.

places.name: Histria
places.summary: The oldest Greek city in Romania, conquered by M. Terentius Varro Lucullus in 72-71 BC; C. Antonius Hybrida was routed near it by the Bastarnae in 61 BC. Silting of its harbour ended it in the 7th century.

places.name: Callatis
places.summary: Dorian colony of Heraclea Pontica whose treaty with Rome (c. 72 BC?) survives on a bronze tablet.

places.name: Odessos
places.summary: Milesian port on the Thracian coast, with the largest Roman bath complex in the Balkans (late 2nd century).

places.name: Marcianopolis
places.foundedNote: founded by Trajan, named after his sister Marciana
places.summary: Valens's base during his Gothic war (367-369). In 376 the comes Lupicinus tried to murder the Gothic leaders at a banquet here, provoking the war that ended at Adrianople.

places.name: Tropaeum Traiani
places.foundedNote: trophy dedicated 109; town founded beside it

status.t: town refounded by Constantine and Licinius

places.summary: Trajan's 40 m victory monument to Mars Ultor (109), with 54 metopes of Romans fighting Dacians and Sarmatians, beside an altar listing c. 3,800 fallen soldiers, perhaps from the disaster of 86 or the battle of 101-102.

places.name: Apulum

status.t: seat of the consular governor of the Three Dacias

places.summary: Fortress of XIII Gemina on the Mureș and capital of the Three Dacias. Two towns grew around it, both colonies by Severus.

places.name: Potaissa
places.summary: Fortress of V Macedonica (168-271) by the salt mines of the Arieș.

places.name: Sarmizegetusa Regia
places.summary: Mountain capital of Decebalus at 1,200 m, with andesite circular sanctuaries and a sun disc. Trajan took it in 106; Decebalus's treasure was found hidden under the river Sargetia (Dio 68.14).

places.name: Colonia Ulpia Traiana Augusta Dacica Sarmizegetusa
places.foundedNote: founded c. 108-110 by D. Terentius Scaurianus
places.summary: Trajan's new capital of Dacia, 40 km from the Dacian royal seat, founded for veterans of the Dacian wars; its founding inscription names the governor Scaurianus.

places.name: Porolissum
places.foundedNote: fort on the north-west Dacian frontier
places.summary: Frontier town and customs post at the gateway into Dacia from the north, with a fort for two cohorts and a limes of towers and ramparts.

places.name: Drobeta
places.foundedNote: fort at the north end of Trajan's bridge
places.summary: North bridgehead of Apollodorus's Danube bridge (103-105), 1,135 m on twenty stone piers, shown on Trajan's Column. Hadrian removed the superstructure; piers still stand.

places.name: Napoca
places.summary: Dacian town made a municipium by Hadrian, later capital of Dacia Porolissensis.

places.name: Romula
places.summary: Capital of Dacia Inferior (Malvensis) on the Olt, where Philip the Arab rebuilt its walls in 248.

places.name: Salona
places.summary: Capital of Dalmatia and its largest city (perhaps 60,000). Julius Nepos ruled from here until murdered in 480. Its refugees moved into Diocletian's palace at Spalatum c. 614.

places.name: Spalatum
places.summary: The 3-hectare fortified retirement palace where Diocletian grew cabbages and died (c. 311-312); his mausoleum became the cathedral and the palace became the city of Split.

places.name: Iader
places.summary: Liburnian port refounded as a Roman colony, walled by Augustus and Tiberius (CIL III 2907).

places.name: Narona
places.summary: Colony on the Neretva whose Augusteum yielded 17 marble imperial statues in 1995.

places.name: Burnum
places.summary: Fortress of XI Claudia and IV Flavia Felix on the Krka, with a rare military amphitheatre.

places.name: Tilurium
places.summary: Fortress of VII on the Cetina guarding the route into the Dalmatian interior after the Great Illyrian revolt.

places.name: Scodra
places.summary: Capital of the Illyrian king Gentius, captured in 30 days in 168 BC by L. Anicius Gallus during the Third Macedonian War.

places.name: Dyrrachium
places.summary: Greek Epidamnos, start of the Via Egnatia and main port of entry from Brundisium. Caesar's attempt to blockade Pompey here in 48 BC with 25 km of lines ended in defeat. Birthplace of Anastasius I.

places.name: Apollonia
places.summary: Greek city at the other head of the Via Egnatia, where the young Octavian was studying in March 44 BC when news of Caesar's murder arrived.

places.name: Philippopolis
places.summary: Thracian Pulpudeva refounded by Philip II. Its stadium and theatre survive; in 250/251 the Goths under Cniva took it after T. Julius Priscus proclaimed himself emperor inside, and massacred, Ammianus says, 100,000.

places.name: Hadrianopolis
places.summary: Hadrian's refoundation of Thracian Uskudama at the Hebrus confluence. Licinius lost to Constantine here in 324; on 9 August 378 Valens died with two-thirds of his army against the Goths outside it.

places.name: Perinthus
places.summary: Samian city on the Propontis, capital of the province of Thrace; renamed Heraclea under the Tetrarchy. Maximinus Daia was defeated by Licinius near it in 313.

places.name: Constantinopolis
places.foundedNote: Megarian Byzantion c. 660 BC; refounded by Constantine, dedicated 11 May 330

status.t: see second only to Rome (Council of Constantinople)

places.summary: Constantine's New Rome on the site of Byzantion, dedicated 11 May 330, with its own senate from the 350s. The Theodosian walls (413) made it impregnable for eight centuries. Justinian rebuilt Hagia Sophia (537) after the Nika riot; it survived the Avar-Persian siege of 626.

places.name: Thessalonica
places.summary: Capital of Roman Macedonia on the Via Egnatia. Galerius built a palace, rotunda and arch here; in 390 Theodosius's troops massacred perhaps 7,000 in the hippodrome, for which Ambrose demanded penance. The cult of St Demetrius defended it against Slav and Avar sieges (586, 615-618).

places.name: Philippi
places.summary: Philip II's mining town on the Via Egnatia, beneath which Antony and Octavian defeated Brutus and Cassius in two battles in October 42 BC. Paul founded his first European church here (c. 49).

places.name: Pella
places.summary: Capital of the Macedonian kings where Aemilius Paullus took the royal treasure after Pydna (168 BC); later a colony.

places.name: Stobi
places.summary: Paeonian town at the Axius-Erigon confluence; a municipium with a theatre and later a rich episcopal basilica and synagogue (with the Polycharmos inscription).

places.name: Nicopolis
places.foundedNote: founded by Octavian c. 29 BC to commemorate Actium
places.summary: 'Victory City' founded on the site of Octavian's camp by forced synoecism of Epirote and Acarnanian towns, with the Actian games. Epictetus taught here after the expulsion of the philosophers (c. 93).

places.name: Actium
places.summary: Cape with a sanctuary of Apollo at the mouth of the Ambracian Gulf, off which Agrippa defeated Antony and Cleopatra on 2 September 31 BC. Octavian enlarged the temple and dedicated ten captured ships.

places.name: Pydna
places.summary: Coastal town near which Aemilius Paullus defeated Perseus on 22 June 168 BC; a lunar eclipse the night before (21 June) dates the battle.

places.name: Corcyra

status.t: Rome's first protectorate across the Adriatic

places.summary: Greek island city that surrendered to Rome in 229 BC during the First Illyrian War, becoming Rome's first foothold east of the Adriatic and a naval base.

places.name: Athenae
places.summary: The university city of the empire. Sulla stormed it on 1 March 86 BC after it backed Mithridates. Hadrian completed the Olympieion and founded the Panhellenion (131-132); the Heruli sacked it in 267; Justinian's ban on pagan teaching in 529 ended the Academy.

places.name: Piraeus
places.summary: Athens' port, whose arsenal of Philo Sulla burned in 86 BC after a siege against Mithridates' general Archelaus. A shipwreck-like cache of bronzes (Piraeus Apollo) was found in 1959.

places.name: Corinthus
places.foundedNote: Greek polis destroyed 146 BC; Colonia Laus Iulia Corinthiensis 44 BC
places.summary: Greek city razed by Mummius in 146 BC, the same year as Carthage, its men killed and women and children sold. Caesar refounded it with freedmen; it became capital of Achaea and Paul stayed 18 months (Gallio inscription at Delphi dates him to c. 51-52).

places.name: Sparta
places.summary: Once leader of Greece, by Roman times a tourist curiosity where youths were flogged at the altar of Artemis Orthia in a theatre built for spectators. Augustus's friend Eurycles ruled it.

places.name: Argos
places.summary: Peloponnesian city where Pyrrhus was killed in street fighting in 272 BC, struck by a roof tile thrown by an old woman.

places.name: Delphi

status.t: Rome takes over from the Aetolians

places.summary: Oracle of Apollo, consulted by Rome after Cannae (Fabius Pictor's embassy, 216 BC). Aemilius Paullus capped Perseus's monument with his own after Pydna. Plutarch served as priest; the oracle was effectively closed under Theodosius.

places.name: Olympia
places.summary: Sanctuary of Zeus where Nero competed in 67, the games having been moved for him, and won the chariot race despite falling out. The games are traditionally said to have ended under Theodosius I (393).

places.name: Delos
places.summary: Apollo's island, made a free port by Rome in 166 BC to ruin Rhodes; Strabo says its slave market could handle 10,000 a day (14.5.2). Sacked in 88 and 69 BC, it never recovered.

places.name: Rhodus

status.t: ruined by the Delian free port

places.summary: Naval republic and Rome's ally against Philip V and Antiochus III, then punished after Pydna by the free port at Delos. Cassius plundered it in 43 BC. Tiberius lived here in self-exile (6 BC-AD 2).

places.name: Patrae
places.foundedNote: Colonia Augusta Aroe Patrensis c. 14 BC
places.summary: Achaean port refounded by Augustus as a veteran colony, the main Greek harbour for Italy. Tradition places the martyrdom of St Andrew here.

places.name: Thebae
places.summary: Boeotian city, a shadow of its 4th-century BC greatness by the time Sulla gave half its land to Delphi.

places.name: Chalcis
places.summary: Euboean city on the Euripus, one of Philip V's 'fetters of Greece' and Antiochus III's winter base in 192-191 BC, where he married a local girl.

places.name: Demetrias
places.foundedNote: founded by Demetrius Poliorcetes c. 294 BC
places.summary: Macedonian royal foundation, another 'fetter of Greece', where Antiochus III landed in 192 BC to start his war with Rome.

places.name: Gortyn
places.summary: Capital of the province of Crete and Cyrene after Metellus Creticus's conquest (69-67 BC). The Gortyn law code (5th century BC) was reused in the wall of the Roman odeum.

places.name: Dodona
places.summary: Oracle of Zeus in the oak. In 167 BC the Senate ordered Aemilius Paullus to sack 70 Epirote towns and enslave 150,000 people, one of the largest enslavements recorded.

places.name: Eleusis
places.summary: Sanctuary of the Mysteries, into which Sulla, Augustus, Hadrian and Marcus Aurelius were initiated. Marcus rebuilt it after the Costoboci raid of 170.

places.name: Epidaurus

status.t: serpent of Asclepius brought to Rome

places.summary: Sanctuary of Asclepius from which an embassy brought the god's serpent to Rome in 292 BC during a plague; it slipped ashore on the Tiber Island, where his temple was built.

places.name: Laurion
places.summary: Athenian silver mines whose slaves revolted c. 104-100 BC, contemporary with the Second Sicilian Slave War. Strabo says by his day the veins were exhausted and only old slag was reworked (9.1.23).
